2025_104_9_a_smith_ms_quote_revised.paragraph: A revised equipment-and-installation quote prepared for Troy Public Schools on 5/28/2025 by JJ Mota covers a new EPIC/SAFE intercom, paging, bell, clock and classroom-audio system at Smith MS. Line items run from the rackmount headend appliance and software licenses through 132 CS-12 plenum-rated ceiling speakers, 40 classroom audio installations, Cat6 cabling, labor and lift/dumpster rentals. The material subtotal is $142,026.00 and the labor subtotal $26,952.00 for a cost subtotal of $168,978.00; with $5,000.00 in shipping and no spares, owner allowance or bond, the quoted total is $173,978.00.

2025_106_pa_146_legislative_overview.paragraph: A 21-slide presentation by Kim St. Martin, Ph.D., Director of the MiMTSS Technical Assistance Center (mimtsstac.org), dated June 2025, walks the Troy Board of Education through Michigan's K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law. Public Acts 146 and 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024; PA 146 revises the 1280f Read by Grade Three statute, extends Individual Reading Improvement Plans across K-3, mandates specified screening measures in K-3 and indicator-triggered screening in grades 4-12, and requires Tier 1 instruction to use a "code-emphasis instructional approach." MDE must update its approved assessment list and publish a list of evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026.
2025_106_pa_146_legislative_overview.page:
**Presentation**: "PA 146 Legislative Overview," PowerPoint, 21 slides, presented to the Troy Board of Education, meeting date June 3, 2025.
**Presenter**: Kim St. Martin, Ph.D., Director, MiMTSS TA Center (mimtsstac.org). **Dated**: June 2025.

**Framing**
Bipartisan laws Public Act 146 and Public Act 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, to improve reading outcomes for K-12 learners, affecting in-service and pre-service teachers. They are frequently called the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law. The law is not focused on diagnosing learners with dyslexia.

**PA 146 components**
PA 146 includes Read by Grade Three, revising the 1280f statute. Individual Reading Improvement Plans (IRIPs) span K-3; 4th grade IRIPs are NOT included, though MDE is examining K-12 language to clarify requirements beyond 3rd grade. IRIP information must be reported to ISDs de-identified, then aggregated and sent to MDE. Diagnostic assessments are no longer referenced, and the term "district-identified coaches" is infused into the language.

**Assessment requirements**
K-3 requires reliable and valid screening and progress monitoring measures for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondences, single-word reading, nonsense word reading, rapid automized naming, oral passage reading fluency, and comprehension (retelling, cloze reading procedure). Rapid Automized Naming (RAN) identifies dyslexia characteristics by timing students naming known colors, objects, letters, or words; teachers should not be asked to teach students to improve RAN data (MDE Dyslexia Handbook).
In grades 4-12, only adolescents showing listed indicators need screening: escape or avoidance behaviors around reading or writing; effortful or laborious reading; comprehension difficulties caused by inaccurate or inefficient word reading; significant spelling or encoding difficulties not caused by fine or visual motor difficulties; low performance on approved English language arts standards or approved standardized literacy assessments; reading deficiency. Those students must be screened with an assessment from MDE's approved list; where data confirm the need for Tier 2 reading intervention support, students need access to intervention and are screened at least three times per year.

**Dyslexia definition and characteristics**
PA 146 defines dyslexia as both (i) a specific learning disorder neurobiological in origin, characterized by difficulties with accurate or fluent word recognition and poor spelling and decoding typically resulting from a deficit in the phonological component of language, often unexpected relative to other cognitive abilities; and (ii) a disorder that may include secondary consequences such as comprehension problems and reduced reading experience impeding vocabulary growth. Characteristics are sampled from Table 1 of the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, pg. 15 — K-3 examples include confusing letters with similar sounds and difficulty with handwriting; grades 4-12 include difficulty reading and spelling multisyllabic words and limited vocabulary.

**MTSS and code emphasis**
The law outlines Tier 1 class-wide reading instruction and adds language on Tier 1 curriculum resources and methods teaching decoding and word recognition through a "code-emphasis instructional approach"; Tiers 2 and 3 cover intensifying intervention. K-3 intervention support must be documented in the IRIP. Code emphasis means direct, explicit instruction on the code system of written English at the sound, syllable, morpheme, and word level so pupils develop automaticity in accurate sound-symbol associations.

**Prohibited methods, Sec. 23c (iii)**
Methods and resources must not minimize using letter-sound information to decode unknown words — including guessing from pictures, skipping words to use passage meaning, guessing from only the first sound, memorizing a word in its written form, and using predictable or leveled text for initial word recognition instruction — unless used to confirm meaning after decoding has been attempted.

**Science of Reading**
Per The Reading League (TRL, 2022), a large body of scientifically-based cross-disciplinary research conducted over the last 50 years worldwide, including multiple languages. It is not an ideology or philosophy, a fad or pendulum swing, a political agenda, one-size-fits-all, a program of instruction, or a single component such as phonics.

**MDE responsibilities**
Provide a coaching model, including expansion to grades 4-12; update a list of assessments by January 1, 2026; publish a list of evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026; and develop Technical Assistance on assessment selection and use, structured literacy, evidence-based methods and materials, and understanding dyslexia.

**Resources listed**
MDE K-12 Literacy and Dyslexia Laws; Section 35m and 35n; K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Research Network; and the 2025 Dyslexia Summit keynote "Building a New Brain City: Connecting Neuroscience & Educational Practices for Students with Reading."
2025_106_pa_146_legislative_overview.verbose:
"PA 146 Legislative Overview" is a 21-slide PowerPoint presented at the Troy Board of Education meeting of June 3, 2025, explaining Michigan's K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law to the board.

PRESENTER AND SOURCE
The deck is authored by Kim St. Martin, Ph.D., identified on the closing slide as Director of the MiMTSS TA Center, and carries the web address mimtsstac.org and the date June 2025. Content is drawn from the statute itself and from the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, and the deck closes with a resources slide and a thank-you slide.

THE LAW
Bipartisan laws Public Act 146 and Public Act 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, with the stated goal of improving reading outcomes for K-12 learners and impacting in-service and pre-service teachers. The pair is frequently referred to as the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law. The presentation emphasizes that the law is not focused on diagnosing learners with dyslexia.

PA 146 COMPONENTS AND THE 1280f REVISION
PA 146 includes Read by Grade Three, revising the 1280f statute. The changes highlighted are: Individual Reading Improvement Plans (IRIPs) now span K-3; developing 4th grade IRIPs is explicitly not included in PA 146, although MDE is examining the language for K-12 to further clarify IRIP requirements beyond 3rd grade; PA 146 requires a level of IRIP information to be reported to ISDs, with student information de-identified, and then aggregated and sent to MDE; diagnostic assessments are no longer referenced; and the term "district-identified coaches" is infused into the language.

K-3 ASSESSMENT REQUIREMENTS
For kindergarten through 3rd grade, reliable and valid screening and progress monitoring assessment measures are required for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondences, single-word reading, nonsense word reading, rapid automized naming, oral passage reading fluency, and comprehension assessment (retelling, cloze reading procedure).

RAPID AUTOMIZED NAMING
A dedicated slide addresses Rapid Automized Naming (RAN). A RAN assessment measure is used to identify dyslexia characteristics. RAN measures cognitive processing speed by asking students to name known colors, objects, letters, or words, and the assessment is timed. The deck states that teachers should not be asked to teach students how to improve their RAN screening assessment data, and cites the MDE Dyslexia Handbook.

GRADES 4-12 ASSESSMENT REQUIREMENTS
Only adolescents who demonstrate any of the listed indicators need a screening assessment to confirm dyslexia consequences. The indicators are: escape or avoidance behaviors when asked to engage in reading or writing activities; effortful or laborious reading; reading comprehension difficulties caused by inaccurate or inefficient word reading; significant spelling or encoding (writing) difficulties not caused by fine or visual motor difficulties; low performance on approved English language arts standards; low performance on approved standardized literacy assessments; and reading deficiency. Students in grades 4-12 demonstrating any of these must be screened using a reliable and valid screening assessment from MDE's approved list. The screening assessment data confirms the need for Tier 2 reading intervention support, and where the data confirm that need, students will need access to reading intervention and will be screened at least three times per year.

DYSLEXIA DEFINITION AS WRITTEN IN PA 146
"Dyslexia" means both of the following: (i) a specific learning disorder that is neurobiological in origin and characterized by difficulties with accurate or fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding abilities that typically result from a deficit in the phonological component of language that is often unexpected in relation to other cognitive abilities and the provision of effective classroom instruction; and (ii) a specific learning disorder that may include secondary consequences, such as problems in reading comprehension and a reduced reading experience that can impede the growth of vocabulary and lead to social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties.

DYSLEXIA CHARACTERISTICS
The characteristics presented are a sample from Table 1 of the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, page 15. For K-3, the listed characteristics are: confuses letters whose sounds are similar; repeatedly misspells words that include letter-sound combinations that have been taught; finds handwriting to be difficult (for example, pencil grip, letter formation); avoids reading-related activities; and difficulty finding the correct word when speaking. For 4th through 12th grade: demonstrates significant difficulties when trying to read and spell multisyllabic words; finds it challenging to understand new information from text due to underlying decoding and word recognition issues; limited vocabulary; lacks written expression skills compared to grade-level peers; and avoids reading and writing activities at school and at home.

MTSS AND TIERED SUPPORT
The law outlines the features of Tier 1, class-wide reading instruction, consistent with a portion of the language that was in the Read by Grade law. New language outlines Tier 1 curriculum resources and instructional methods to teach decoding and word recognition using a "code-emphasis instructional approach." Tiers 2 and 3 outline the methods to intensify literacy intervention instruction. Students in K-3 who need intervention support must have that support documented in the Individual Reading Improvement Plan. The deck notes that the term Individual Reading Intervention Plan is also used in PA 146 and that MDE will be clarifying how to interpret the language. The MDE web address WWW.MICHIGAN.GOV/MDE appears on this slide.

CODE-EMPHASIS INSTRUCTIONAL APPROACH DEFINED
"Code emphasis means direct, explicit instruction on the code system of written English at the sound, syllable, morpheme, and word level so pupils develop automaticity in accurate sound-symbol associations used for word recognition and for developing a robust sight-word vocabulary."

SCIENCE OF READING
Citing The Reading League (TRL, 2022), the Science of Reading is described as a large body of scientifically-based research across disciplines about reading and issues related to reading and writing; research conducted over the last 50 years across the world; and research that includes findings from studies in learning to read in multiple languages. The Science of Reading means there is substantial evidence to inform how proficient reading and writing develop, why some have difficulty, and how we can most effectively assess and teach to improve outcomes. A companion slide lists what the Science of Reading is not: not an ideology or philosophy; not a fad, trend, new idea, or pendulum swing; not a political agenda; not a one-size-fits-all approach; not a program of instruction; and not a single, specific component of instruction, such as phonics.

PROHIBITED INSTRUCTIONAL METHODS UNDER SEC. 23c (iii)
The statutory text quoted states that the instructional methods and curriculum resources described in that subparagraph must not include instructional methods or curriculum resources that minimize the importance of primarily using letter-sound information to decode or recognize unknown words, including but not limited to the following, unless used to confirm the meaning of unknown words after decoding has been attempted: (A) prompting pupils to guess unknown words using pictures and illustrations; (B) skipping over an unknown word or words to use the meaning of the passage to recognize the unknown word or words; (C) identifying only the first sound of an unknown word and then being prompted to guess the word using the word's initial sound and the meaning of the text surrounding the word; (D) memorizing a word in its written form; and (E) using predictable text and leveled text to provide initial word recognition instruction and practice in reading new learned letter-sound correspondences.

MDE RESPONSIBILITIES
As a result of this law, the Michigan Department of Education is required to: provide a coaching model, including expanding a coaching model to grades 4-12; update a list of assessments by January 1, 2026; publish a list of evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026; and develop Technical Assistance (TA) covering the selection and use of assessments (universal screener and progress monitoring assessments), structured literacy, evidence-based instructional method and curriculum materials, and understanding dyslexia.

RESOURCES CITED
The resources slide lists MDE K-12 Literacy and Dyslexia Laws; Section 35m and 35n; the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Research Network; and the keynote from the 2025 Dyslexia Summit titled "Building a New Brain City: Connecting Neuroscience & Educational Practices for Students with Reading." A Questions slide precedes the resources, and the final slide reads "Thank YOU!" with the presenter's name and title, Director, MiMTSS TA Center.

MDE must update its approved assessment list and publish evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026.

It is not an ideology or philosophy, a fad or pendulum swing, a political agenda, one-size-fits-all, a program of instruction, or a single component such as phonics.

**MDE responsibilities**
Provide a coaching model, including expansion to grades 4-12; update a list of assessments by January 1, 2026; publish a list of evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026; and develop Technical Assistance on assessment selection and use, structured literacy, evidence-based methods and materials, and understanding dyslexia.

**Resources listed**
MDE K-12 Literacy and Dyslexia Laws; Section 35m and 35n; K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Research Network; and the 2025 Dyslexia Summit keynote "Building a New Brain City: Connecting Neuroscience & Educational Practices for Students with Reading."
2025_107_pa_146_legislative_overview.verbose:
"PA 146 Legislative Overview" is the PDF rendering of a 21-page slide deck presented at the Troy Board of Education meeting of June 3, 2025, explaining Michigan's K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law. Its content matches the PowerPoint version distributed with the same agenda.

PRESENTER AND SOURCE
The deck is authored by Kim St. Martin, Ph.D., identified on the closing slide as Director of the MiMTSS TA Center, and carries the web address mimtsstac.org and the date June 2025. Content is drawn from the statute itself and from the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, and the deck closes with a resources slide and a thank-you slide.

THE LAW
Bipartisan laws Public Act 146 and Public Act 147 of 2024 were signed by Governor Whitmer on October 10, 2024, with the stated goal of improving reading outcomes for K-12 learners and impacting in-service and pre-service teachers. The pair is frequently referred to as the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Law. The presentation emphasizes that the law is not focused on diagnosing learners with dyslexia.

PA 146 COMPONENTS AND THE 1280f REVISION
PA 146 includes Read by Grade Three, revising the 1280f statute. The changes highlighted are: Individual Reading Improvement Plans (IRIPs) now span K-3; developing 4th grade IRIPs is explicitly not included in PA 146, although MDE is examining the language for K-12 to further clarify IRIP requirements beyond 3rd grade; PA 146 requires a level of IRIP information to be reported to ISDs, with student information de-identified, and then aggregated and sent to MDE; diagnostic assessments are no longer referenced; and the term "district-identified coaches" is infused into the language.

K-3 ASSESSMENT REQUIREMENTS
For kindergarten through 3rd grade, reliable and valid screening and progress monitoring assessment measures are required for phonemic awareness, letter-sound correspondences, single-word reading, nonsense word reading, rapid automized naming, oral passage reading fluency, and comprehension assessment (retelling, cloze reading procedure).

RAPID AUTOMIZED NAMING
A dedicated slide addresses Rapid Automized Naming (RAN). A RAN assessment measure is used to identify dyslexia characteristics. RAN measures cognitive processing speed by asking students to name known colors, objects, letters, or words, and the assessment is timed. The deck states that teachers should not be asked to teach students how to improve their RAN screening assessment data, and cites the MDE Dyslexia Handbook.

GRADES 4-12 ASSESSMENT REQUIREMENTS
Only adolescents who demonstrate any of the listed indicators need a screening assessment to confirm dyslexia consequences. The indicators are: escape or avoidance behaviors when asked to engage in reading or writing activities; effortful or laborious reading; reading comprehension difficulties caused by inaccurate or inefficient word reading; significant spelling or encoding (writing) difficulties not caused by fine or visual motor difficulties; low performance on approved English language arts standards; low performance on approved standardized literacy assessments; and reading deficiency. Students in grades 4-12 demonstrating any of these must be screened using a reliable and valid screening assessment from MDE's approved list. The screening assessment data confirms the need for Tier 2 reading intervention support, and where the data confirm that need, students will need access to reading intervention and will be screened at least three times per year.

DYSLEXIA DEFINITION AS WRITTEN IN PA 146
"Dyslexia" means both of the following: (i) a specific learning disorder that is neurobiological in origin and characterized by difficulties with accurate or fluent word recognition and by poor spelling and decoding abilities that typically result from a deficit in the phonological component of language that is often unexpected in relation to other cognitive abilities and the provision of effective classroom instruction; and (ii) a specific learning disorder that may include secondary consequences, such as problems in reading comprehension and a reduced reading experience that can impede the growth of vocabulary and lead to social, emotional, and behavioral difficulties.

DYSLEXIA CHARACTERISTICS
The characteristics presented are a sample from Table 1 of the MDE Dyslexia Handbook, page 15. For K-3, the listed characteristics are: confuses letters whose sounds are similar; repeatedly misspells words that include letter-sound combinations that have been taught; finds handwriting to be difficult (for example, pencil grip, letter formation); avoids reading-related activities; and difficulty finding the correct word when speaking. For 4th through 12th grade: demonstrates significant difficulties when trying to read and spell multisyllabic words; finds it challenging to understand new information from text due to underlying decoding and word recognition issues; limited vocabulary; lacks written expression skills compared to grade-level peers; and avoids reading and writing activities at school and at home.

MTSS AND TIERED SUPPORT
The law outlines the features of Tier 1, class-wide reading instruction, consistent with a portion of the language that was in the Read by Grade law. New language outlines Tier 1 curriculum resources and instructional methods to teach decoding and word recognition using a "code-emphasis instructional approach." Tiers 2 and 3 outline the methods to intensify literacy intervention instruction. Students in K-3 who need intervention support must have that support documented in the Individual Reading Improvement Plan. The deck notes that the term Individual Reading Intervention Plan is also used in PA 146 and that MDE will be clarifying how to interpret the language. The MDE web address WWW.MICHIGAN.GOV/MDE appears on this slide.

CODE-EMPHASIS INSTRUCTIONAL APPROACH DEFINED
"Code emphasis means direct, explicit instruction on the code system of written English at the sound, syllable, morpheme, and word level so pupils develop automaticity in accurate sound-symbol associations used for word recognition and for developing a robust sight-word vocabulary."

SCIENCE OF READING
Citing The Reading League (TRL, 2022), the Science of Reading is described as a large body of scientifically-based research across disciplines about reading and issues related to reading and writing; research conducted over the last 50 years across the world; and research that includes findings from studies in learning to read in multiple languages. The Science of Reading means there is substantial evidence to inform how proficient reading and writing develop, why some have difficulty, and how we can most effectively assess and teach to improve outcomes. A companion slide lists what the Science of Reading is not: not an ideology or philosophy; not a fad, trend, new idea, or pendulum swing; not a political agenda; not a one-size-fits-all approach; not a program of instruction; and not a single, specific component of instruction, such as phonics.

PROHIBITED INSTRUCTIONAL METHODS UNDER SEC. 23c (iii)
The statutory text quoted states that the instructional methods and curriculum resources described in that subparagraph must not include instructional methods or curriculum resources that minimize the importance of primarily using letter-sound information to decode or recognize unknown words, including but not limited to the following, unless used to confirm the meaning of unknown words after decoding has been attempted: (A) prompting pupils to guess unknown words using pictures and illustrations; (B) skipping over an unknown word or words to use the meaning of the passage to recognize the unknown word or words; (C) identifying only the first sound of an unknown word and then being prompted to guess the word using the word's initial sound and the meaning of the text surrounding the word; (D) memorizing a word in its written form; and (E) using predictable text and leveled text to provide initial word recognition instruction and practice in reading new learned letter-sound correspondences.

MDE RESPONSIBILITIES
As a result of this law, the Michigan Department of Education is required to: provide a coaching model, including expanding a coaching model to grades 4-12; update a list of assessments by January 1, 2026; publish a list of evidence-based Tier 1 reading curricula and materials by January 1, 2026; and develop Technical Assistance (TA) covering the selection and use of assessments (universal screener and progress monitoring assessments), structured literacy, evidence-based instructional method and curriculum materials, and understanding dyslexia.

RESOURCES CITED
The resources slide lists MDE K-12 Literacy and Dyslexia Laws; Section 35m and 35n; the K-12 Literacy/Dyslexia Research Network; and the keynote from the 2025 Dyslexia Summit titled "Building a New Brain City: Connecting Neuroscience & Educational Practices for Students with Reading." A Questions slide precedes the resources, and the final slide reads "Thank YOU!" with the presenter's name and title, Director, MiMTSS TA Center.
